title: Lakshmana wounded
hook: two torches crossing a battlefield at night, and an old bear's surprising question

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana wounded, and Rama beside him. They chose to endure Brahma's weapon, and fell with much of the army. Did you try accepting something you couldn't fight? Tonight, two survivors walk the field. Day six hundred forty-eight.

Two people are still on their feet. Vibhishana, who knows the weapons of Lanka, and Hanuman. It's night. They take torches and walk out across the battlefield, stepping between fallen warriors, looking for anyone still alive. Rama and Lakshmana lie in the arrows. Leader after leader lies still. And then, in the torchlight, they find Jambavan, the old king of the bears, so pierced with arrows he can't open his eyes, still breathing.
screen: `TWO STILL STANDING.` → `TORCHES ACROSS THE FIELD.` → `JAMBAVAN, STILL BREATHING.`

segments.voice: Vibhishana kneels and asks if he's alive. Jambavan knows the voice, though he can't see. And his first question isn't about Rama, or Lakshmana, or Sugriva his king. It's this: is Hanuman alive? Vibhishana is puzzled. Why ask about Hanuman, and not the princes? Jambavan's answer is one of the great lines of the war. If Hanuman lives, he says, then the whole army lives, even if it has been killed. If Hanuman is dead, then we're dead, even though we're still breathing. Hanuman steps forward and bows at the old bear's feet. And Jambavan, revived by the sound of him, gives his orders. Go north, over the ocean, to the Himalaya. Between Mount Rishabha and Mount Kailasa there's a mountain covered with healing herbs. He names four of them. One that brings back life. One that draws out arrows. One that restores the body's color. One that joins what's broken. Bring them back, Jambavan says, and the army will rise. Why does Jambavan ask about Hanuman first? Because he's thinking like an elder. Who can still act tonight? Who can cross a sea and come back before dawn? Grief would ask about the princes first. Wisdom asks about the one who can save them. And it's Jambavan, you may remember, who once reminded Hanuman of his own strength, before the great leap to Lanka. Now, on a dark field, he does it again.
screen: `IS HANUMAN ALIVE?` · `IF HE LIVES, WE ALL LIVE.` · `FOUR HERBS ON A HIMALAYAN PEAK.` · `WISDOM ASKS WHO CAN ACT.` · then, large: `THE OLD BEAR SENDS HIM AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Think of a hard situation around you right now, at home or at work. Instead of asking whose fault it is, or who's hurt most, ask Jambavan's question: who can still act? Maybe it's a friend, maybe a professional, maybe you. Picture them standing in the torchlight. Breathe in steadiness. Breathe out panic. The bell holds the time.
Lakshmana wounded. While the princes lie in the arrows, Jambavan asks first whether Hanuman lives, and sends him north for four herbs.
Your line: Lakshmana wounded. Today, in one tangle, ask who can still act, and start there. Day six hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Jambavan's question, is Hanuman alive, is often retold by devotees of Hanuman as a sign of his place in the Ramayana, and Hanuman is widely prayed to by Hindus in times of illness and crisis.

fork.setup: you're Jambavan, wounded and blind on the battlefield at night. you hear a friend's voice. what's your first question?
fork.reveal: he asks about Hanuman: if Hanuman lives, the army lives even though slain; if he's dead, they're dead though living.

original.note: Sanskrit Jāmbavān: the old king of the bears, an elder of the army, also called Jāmbavat.

trapdoor: what you thought: the old bear just wanted news of his friend.
what it means: Jambavan asks who can still act; if Hanuman lives, the army can live.
what a scholar hears: Jambavan's four herbs are named in Valmiki: mṛtasañjīvanī, viśalyakaraṇī, sāvarṇyakaraṇī and sandhānī.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 74 (the night search; Jambavan's question; the four herbs)

notes: Sarga number follows the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
